headline: Efficiency gets more output from less input—often the cheapest and cleanest energy is what you don't use
universal_truth: Reduction often beats production; not needing something is better than having more of it
fun_facts: LED lights use 75% less energy than incandescent bulbs for the same light output
Better insulation can cut heating costs by 50%—without generating any new energy
The US economy produces twice the GDP per unit of energy compared to 1970
discussion_questions: Where could you get more output from the same input—or same output from less?
What are you wasting that efficiency could recover?
When is reducing demand better than increasing supply?

hook.script: The cheapest kilowatt is the one you don't use. Efficiency gets you the same result with less input—same light from less electricity, same comfort from less heating. Before producing more, ask: could you need less?

cliff.script: We often focus on production—make more, get more. But efficiency is equally powerful. Why is reduction undervalued?

options.text: Production is visible, reduction is invisible—we celebrate new things more than optimized things; but not needing something is often better than having more of it
options.response: Yes. Building a power plant is dramatic. Insulating buildings is boring. But they can achieve the same result—and efficiency is often cheaper, cleaner, and faster. Invisible solutions are still solutions.
It does, but we're usually far from those limits—significant gains remain available...

fact1.title: Same Output, Less Input
fact1.script: Efficiency isn't sacrifice—it's optimization. LED lights aren't dimmer; they're smarter. Efficient cars aren't slower; they're better designed. More from less, not less from less.

fact2.title: Cheapest and Cleanest
fact2.script: Energy you don't use has no cost, no pollution, no infrastructure needs. Efficiency is often the fastest, cheapest, cleanest solution. But it's invisible, so it gets less attention.

fact3.title: Personal Efficiency
fact3.script: You can be more efficient too—in time, money, energy. Before asking 'how do I get more?', ask 'how do I need less?' Reducing demand often beats increasing supply.

wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Reduction often beats production. Not needing something is better than having more of it. Consider efficiency before expansion.

outro.script: That's Day 278. Tomorrow, we'll explore making less trash—waste reduction. Until then, find one area where efficiency could help.

growTrack.title: Efficiency Scan - Where Can You Need Less?
growTrack.learning_objective: Identify efficiency opportunities before seeking more
growTrack.activity: Where are you inefficient—wasting time, money, energy, attention? Before seeking more resources, could you use existing resources better? Efficiency gains are often easier, cheaper, and faster than acquiring more.
